units.text: ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ can compare file names, or parts of file names, to shell patterns. A ⟦2⟧shell pattern⟦3⟧ is a string that may contain the following special characters, which are known as ⟦4⟧wildcards⟦5⟧ or ⟦6⟧metacharacters⟦7⟧.
units.sourceHTML: find and locate can compare file names, or parts of file names, to shell patterns. A shell pattern is a string that may contain the following special characters, which are known as wildcards or metacharacters.

units.text: You must quote patterns that contain metacharacters to prevent the shell from expanding them itself. Double and single quotes both work; so does escaping with a backslash.
units.sourceHTML: You must quote patterns that contain metacharacters to prevent the shell from expanding them itself. Double and single quotes both work; so does escaping with a backslash.

units.text: Matches any zero or more characters.

Matches exactly one character that is a member of the string ⟦0⟧. This is called a ⟦1⟧character class⟦2⟧. As a shorthand, ⟦3⟧ may contain ranges, which consist of two characters with a dash between them. For example, the class ‘⟦4⟧’ matches a lowercase letter, a number, or an underscore. You can negate a class by placing a ‘⟦5⟧’ or ‘⟦6⟧’ immediately after the opening bracket. Thus, ‘⟦7⟧’ matches any character except an uppercase letter or an at sign.
units.sourceHTML: Matches exactly one character that is a member of the string string. This is called a character class. As a shorthand, string may contain ranges, which consist of two characters with a dash between them. For example, the class ‘[a-z0-9_]’ matches a lowercase letter, a number, or an underscore. You can negate a class by placing a ‘!’ or ‘^’ immediately after the opening bracket. Thus, ‘[^A-Z@]’ matches any character except an uppercase letter or an at sign.

units.text: Removes the special meaning of the character that follows it. This works even in character classes.
units.sourceHTML: Removes the special meaning of the character that follows it. This works even in character classes.

units.text: In the ⟦0⟧ tests that do shell pattern matching (‘⟦1⟧’, ‘⟦2⟧’, etc.), wildcards in the pattern will match a ‘⟦3⟧’ at the beginning of a file name. This is also the case for ⟦4⟧. Thus, ‘⟦5⟧’ will match a file named ⟦6⟧, as will ‘⟦7⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: In the find tests that do shell pattern matching (‘-name’, ‘-wholename’, etc.), wildcards in the pattern will match a ‘.’ at the beginning of a file name. This is also the case for locate. Thus, ‘find -name '*macs'’ will match a file named .emacs, as will ‘locate '*macs'’.

units.text: Slash characters have no special significance in the shell pattern matching that ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ do, unlike in the shell, in which wildcards do not match them. Therefore, a pattern ‘⟦2⟧’ can match a file name ‘⟦3⟧’, and a pattern ‘⟦4⟧’ can match a file name ‘⟦5⟧’.
units.sourceHTML: Slash characters have no special significance in the shell pattern matching that find and locate do, unlike in the shell, in which wildcards do not match them. Therefore, a pattern ‘foo*bar’ can match a file name ‘foo3/bar’, and a pattern ‘./sr*sc’ can match a file name ‘./src/misc’.

units.text: If you want to locate some files with the ‘⟦0⟧’ command but don’t need to see the full list you can use the ‘⟦1⟧’ option to see just a small number of results, or the ‘⟦2⟧’ option to display only the total number of matches.
units.sourceHTML: If you want to locate some files with the ‘locate’ command but don’t need to see the full list you can use the ‘--limit’ option to see just a small number of results, or the ‘--count’ option to display only the total number of matches.
